title: Annotatio II §.V: Bertram knows only two opinions — spiritual vs corporal-by-conversion; no silent third
pass_a_gloss: And Bertram nearly puts the same beyond doubt when at the start of his book (pp. m. 3, 55) he remembers only two opinions in his time on the presence of Christ’s body in the sacred Supper — of which the one, on Spiritual presence, he himself fosters with the Fathers of all ages; the other, on Corporal [presence] brought in by Conversion of the bread, he fights in Paschasius Radbertus; a Third, if there had been a novel one, he would hardly have passed in silence, especially one to be found in his adversary.
pass_b_english: Bertram nearly settles it: in his day he knows only two opinions — spiritual presence (his own, with the Fathers of every age) versus corporal presence by conversion of the bread (Paschasius), which he attacks.
Had there been a novel third (consubstantiation), he would not have passed it in silence — least of all in his adversary.
source_text: Et tantùm non extra dubium idem ponente Bertramô, quando duarum duntaxat, tempore suo, de praesentia corporis Christi in sacra Coena, sententiarum meminit, initio libri sui pag. m. 3. 55. quarum alteram, de Spirituali praesentia, ipsemet, cum Patribus omnium seculorum, fovet, alteram, de Corporali, per Conversionem panis, adductam, in Paschasio Rhadeberto, oppugnat; Tertiam, si quae fuisset novitiamque, silentio haud praetervecturus, praesertim apud adversarium reperiundam.

choices.english: would hardly have passed in silence
rejected: would hardly have driven past in silence

notes: Bertram only two opinions; no silent third.
